pr_body:
See https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/issues/54313#issuecomment-863347311 and https://github.com/dotnet/maui/issues/822#issuecomment-863323985

The code that initialized `System.IO.PathInternal.s_isCaseSensitive` did I/O in the temp folder to check for case sensitivity.  This is a startup perf hit on Android where low-end devices may have very slow storage. It also returns results that may be misleading since different paths on Unix may have different filesystems mounted that have different case sensitivity (a common case on Android is ext4 for internal storage and exFAT for the SD card).

Instead, return a constant value based on the common platform behavior - case insensitive on Windows and Apple platforms, case sensitive elsewhere.

Also remove `Path.IsCaseSensitive` and `Path.StringComparison` - callers should use `PathInternal` properties directly.

Fixes https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/issues/54339

Would this make sense to hardcode this for all mobile targets ? (e.g. have two files - `*.CaseSensitive.cs` and `*.CaseInsensitive.cs` and include them as appropriate).

> I'm not sure why there is similar logic in Path class as well

The behavior is actually hardcoded in Path class for all platforms:

https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/01b7e73cd378145264a7cb7a09365b41ed42b240/src/libraries/System.Private.CoreLib/src/System/IO/Path.Unix.cs#L137

The reason for this duplication is that there is no public `Path.IsCaseSensitive` property, but this property is needed by outside of CoreLib. PathInternal is included by outside of CoreLib to get access to `IsCaseSensitive` and several other internal properties.

We should make the logic in PathInternal to be hardcoded in the same way as the logic in Path. It helps with both performance and consistency. The check in PathInternal will need to be dynamic (using `OperatingSystem.Is*`).

I'm following along with most of the discussion, but I don't understand this part @jkotas:

>  The check in PathInternal will need to be dynamic (using OperatingSystem.Is*).

Aren't we talking about doing the same thing in PathInternal as in Path: just hardcode based on the common behavior of the underlying OS?  Why would it need to be a dynamic check if we know which RID we're targeting?

@lambdageek because the file is shared as a compilation file you cannot assume that the assembly where the file is included is multi-targeting (has RID specific builds). OperatingSystem properties are static constants so I don't think there will be any perf hit.

Ok, updated to return constants for some known `OperatingSystem.IsXYZ` values.  I left the probing in place as the last case (so non-Android Linux, Windows, FreeBSD and "none of the above" will still do the I/O probing)

I do not think we should be doing any probing. The IsCaseInsensitive property on Path is not doing any probing, and it better be in sync with the property on PathInternal. The probing on PathInternal can only ever lead to inconsistent behavior.
Should we backport this to .NET 6 Preview 6?  (It's not critical for MAUI on Android - they mitigated the perf hit on their end)

> Should we backport this to .NET 6 Preview 6?

If the perf issue was mitigated, I don't think we need to.

review_comments:
Is this going to break if I pass `FILE_FLAG_POSIX_SEMANTICS` to `CreateFile` or if I modify a folder to set it as case insensitive using `fsutil` (which is supported since Win10 17134)?

There are multiple ways to force Windows to be case sensitive, including for the WSL mounted drive, which is fully browsable via File explorer and can be interacted with via the file system APIs

https://devblogs.microsoft.com/commandline/per-directory-case-sensitivity-and-wsl/ goes into some more details about various changes that went in, but even prior to this NTFS has always supported case sensitivity. Its just that Windows hadn't handled it as "first class" if you enabled it.
It will be just as broken as before (when we probed the Temp folder, which is not a good proxy for the behavior of a _specific_ directory - neither on Unix nor on Windows), but faster.

This has been a global setting, independent on the path. This logic is broken if you have parts of the file system configured differently. This PR does not change it. Yes, it would be nice to fix that.

The unmanaged side of the runtime has similar global setting. It is larger problem than just what you can see in the managed libraries.
